title: Skipper-CCD multi-pass sensing reads sub-femtofarad cells
idea: Revive 1970s CCD memory together with the skipper output amplifier. After the access gate opens, the cell's charge packet is clocked back and forth between two transfer gates under a floating-gate electrometer and read non-destructively 16-64 times, then averaged. Noise falls by sqrt(N), so a 1 fF storage node (~6,000 electrons at 1 V) still resolves cleanly.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and destructive read (fact 8). Cs can drop ~4-5x, so pillar aspect ratio can fall from 60-75:1 toward ~20:1. Multi-pass reads add latency, so this suits capacity tiers.

title: Superregenerative quench latch converts bitline signal into time
idea: Borrow Armstrong's 1922 superregenerative receiver. The sense latch is biased just past instability and quenched every cycle, so the tiny bitline differential grows exponentially and its time-to-threshold is proportional to ln(signal). A 6-bit time-to-digital counter at the mat edge decodes 2-bit-per-cell levels from one latch, with no ADC ladder.
why: Enables multi-level DRAM (2 bits/cell) at existing sense-amp pitch: ~2x bits per capacitor and half the sense amps per bit (fact 7 periphery share, fact 1 charge wall).

title: Parametron phase-locked sense amps immune to transistor offset
idea: Revive Goto's 1954 parametron. Each sense node is a tiny resonator (MOS varactor plus active inductor) pumped at 2f, which can only oscillate in one of two phases, and the bitline's charge-sharing signal seeds which phase wins. The decision depends on the seed's sign relative to a common pump rather than on matched transistor pairs, and phase outputs can be majority-voted (parametron logic) for free in-periphery error voting.
why: Large matched sense pairs are no longer needed, so the sense stripe could shrink ~2-3x (fact 7) and work with smaller signals (fact 1).

title: Flying-spot optical wordline addressing replaces drivers and pumps
idea: Modernize the Williams-tube flying-spot scanner. A backside micro-LED or waveguide-grating array lights one row of photogated access-transistor gate lines, and a stacked photovoltaic diode string on each subarray gate line supplies the gate overdrive, replacing the VPP pump. The CMOS row decoder becomes a light-source driver on a separate cheap die.
why: Removes row decoders, sub-wordline drivers and VPP charge pumps (a large part of the 49% periphery, fact 7) and takes the 3 V wordline off the logic node (fact 10).

title: Quadruplex telegraph bitlines carry two cells per sense event
idea: Copy Edison's 1874 quadruplex telegraph, which sent one message as current polarity and another as amplitude on a single wire. Two cells on paired rows share one bitline event: one dumps charge through its normal access device, and the other is read through a 2x plate-line pulse that injects a doubly weighted, opposite-polarity charge. A 4-level sense (two latches with offset references) decodes both bits.
why: Halves sense amps per bit and halves activation events per bit read (facts 7, 8): ~1.6x periphery density.

title: Harmonic-telegraph frequency-division global data lines
idea: Revive Bell's and Gray's harmonic telegraph. Each subarray's secondary sense output modulates its own on-chip tone (1-8 GHz, from an injection-locked ring oscillator) onto one shared global data line, and the I/O block separates the channels with passive N-path filters. Eight banks' data share one wire instead of eight.
why: Cuts global data-bus wires and repeaters ~4-8x (fact 7 periphery area) and lets more banks run in parallel without adding wire area (fact 5).

title: PRML read channel undoes bitline crosstalk instead of shielding
idea: Port the partial-response maximum-likelihood detection IBM introduced for magnetic disks in 1990. Groups of 8 adjacent bitlines are sampled by 3-bit flash comparators after charge sharing, and a small Viterbi detector decides the bits jointly using the die's measured coupling matrix. Inter-bitline crosstalk becomes a modeled channel instead of noise that has to be shielded or twisted away.
why: Allows ~30% tighter bitline pitch or ~40% less signal margin (facts 1, 4), trading a little periphery logic for array density.

title: Plasma-panel sustain waveform refreshes cells without sensing
idea: AC plasma displays (1964) held every pixel with nothing but a global sustain pulse and wall-charge bistability. Give each cell a series threshold-switching selector (e.g., NbOx) to a global pulsed sustain rail: cells still above threshold (decaying 1s) conduct and are topped up, and cells near zero stay off. The whole array refreshes in one global pulse, with no row activation and no sense amp.
why: Eliminates refresh activations (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) and the refresh counter and scheduler logic; claims >10x lower refresh energy.

title: Nanocryotron sense amps for 4-kelvin DRAM
idea: Revive Buck's 1956 cryotron in its modern form, the superconducting nanowire nTron. At 4 K a DRAM cell retains data for hours, and an NbN nanowire biased near its critical current switches to the normal state when the bitline's charge-sharing current adds to it, giving >1,000x gain at zero static power. Decoders become nTron trees, which removes CMOS periphery heat from the cold stage.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and slashes sense energy for quantum and superconducting computers, which lack dense cold memory today. Niche, but no incumbent holds it.

title: Ferreed-style latching microswitches for zero-standby bank gating
idea: Bell System's 1960 ferreed crosspoint used remanent magnetization to latch a reed contact, so it held its state with zero power. Build BEOL electrostatic microcontacts clamped closed by HZO remanent polarization, and use them to disconnect idle banks' periphery from the supply and to steer spare rows, with no holding power and no leakage when open.
why: Cuts periphery standby leakage in gated banks ~100x (idle power, fact 3 context) and replaces fuse-latch steering logic (fact 7).

title: Rosen piezoelectric transformer generates wordline voltage acoustically
idea: Revive the 1950s Rosen piezoelectric transformer as an AlN MEMS resonator in the package or interposer (AlN is CMOS-compatible and made in the U.S.). Driven at resonance from 1.1 V, it steps the voltage up acoustically to 3-4 V and replaces on-die Dickson charge pumps for the VPP and negative-wordline rails.
why: Frees the ~5-8% of die area spent on charge pumps and their decoupling (fact 7) and lifts VPP conversion efficiency from ~30% to ~70% (fact 10 energy).

title: Diode-matrix predecoders printed in BEOL above the array
idea: 1950s computers decoded addresses with passive diode matrices. Deposit a thin-film oxide Schottky diode stack (e.g., Pt/IGZO) between upper metals and wire it as a diode-AND predecode matrix directly over the cell array, so the silicon below holds only the final wordline drivers.
why: Moves ~30-40% of decoder logic off silicon, shrinking the periphery share (fact 7) by several points without EUV (fact 4).

title: Delay-line recirculating 3D string refreshes data by circulation
idea: As in mercury delay lines and drums, data in a vertical 3D DRAM string never sits still. The tiers are charge-coupled gates, and charge packets shift one tier per clock past a single regenerating sense amp at the string base, which restores each packet as it passes. No lateral access transistor is needed per tier, and refresh comes free with the circulation.
why: Attacks fact 2 (the lateral transistor blocks 3D) and fact 3 (refresh). One sense amp serves a 64-128-tier string. Random-access latency rises, so it fits capacity or streaming tiers.

title: Twistor helical vertical bitlines cancel 3D coupling noise
idea: The twistor wound magnetic tape helically around a wire to define its sensing path. Shift each vertical 3D DRAM bitline a quarter pitch at every tier step, so it climbs in a staircase helix and spends equal length beside each neighbor. Coupling then becomes common-mode, which the differential sense amp rejects.
why: Cuts inter-bitline coupling noise ~3-5x in 3D stacks (fact 2), allowing smaller signals and more tiers per sense amp.

title: Transfluxor-style ferroelectric column gate eliminates repair comparators
idea: The 1956 transfluxor used flux stored around a control aperture to block or pass transfer through a second aperture. Put one HZO ferroelectric FET in series with each column-select line. Programmed at wafer test, a bad column's FeFET stays permanently off and its spare's turns on, so column repair needs no fuse-address comparators in the read path.
why: Removes column-redundancy compare logic and fuse latches (fact 7) and shaves ~0.5-1 ns off the column access path.

title: Neuristor Mott lines self-regenerate global wordlines
idea: Revive Crane's 1960 neuristor, an active line that propagates pulses without loss. NbO2 Mott-threshold elements with local shunt capacitors are spaced along long global wordlines and data lines, so the pulse re-fires at each element the way an action potential travels down an axon, and no CMOS repeaters are needed.
why: Removes repeater and buffer stripes (fact 7) and cuts energy on long global lines ~2x (fact 5).

title: Acoustic delay-line page buffer frees sense amps instantly
idea: A modern mercury delay line: an AlN surface-acoustic-wave track runs under each bank's I/O edge. A sensed row is launched as acoustic pulses that take ~100 ns to cross, during which the sense amps precharge and open the next row; a transducer at the far end recaptures the bits as they arrive and serves bursts in flight.
why: Hides precharge and row-cycle time and replaces SRAM row caches in the periphery, for ~1.5x effective bank bandwidth on streaming loads.

title: Vibrating-reed electrometer screens leakage-tail cells in milliseconds
idea: The 1940s vibrating-reed electrometer measured femtoamps by modulating a capacitor mechanically. A varactor-modulated test capacitor on each mat's test bus measures each row's integrated leakage directly by lock-in detection in milliseconds, replacing hours-long hot retention tests. Rows are then binned into 2-4 refresh classes stored on the die.
why: Enables per-row refresh where today the ≤13 fA tail forces worst-case refresh for every row (fact 3), cutting refresh ~60-75%, and slashes test time.

title: Pilot-tone automatic gain control lowers array voltage
idea: Like the AGC in 1930s tube radios: each activation also reads two pilot cells (a known 1 and a known 0) on dedicated bitlines, and their sensed amplitude sets the main sense amps' latch-enable delay and reference trim in real time. Margin tracks temperature and aging directly, so VARY can drop from ~1.0 V toward 0.7 V without worst-case guardbands.
why: Attacks the voltage floor (fact 10): CV² array energy falls ~50% at 0.7 V, for 2 extra bitlines per ~1k.

title: Equivalent-time sampling scope built into each sense stripe
idea: 1960s sampling oscilloscopes captured GHz waveforms by sampling repeated events at slipping delays. Add one sampling switch and comparator per sense stripe; across repeated activations it reconstructs the real bitline charge-sharing waveform, and boot firmware sets each mat's tRCD and sense-enable timing from it.
why: Removes worst-case timing guardbands: ~15-25% lower tRCD/tRAS and better yield of slow mats (facts 1, 4).

title: Core-stack business model: periphery wafers from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Core memory was sold as a woven stack from one vendor and a driver/sense chassis from another. Split DRAM the same way: array-only wafers (cells and bitlines, no periphery) from existing DRAM fabs are hybrid-bonded to periphery wafers built on depreciated 28-40 nm U.S. logic lines, creating a merchant market for memory periphery.
why: Array dies gain ~1.6x bits per leading-edge wafer by shedding the 49% periphery (fact 7), and more of the value is made in the U.S. on existing tools (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Smart-pixel free-space optical page readout to processor
idea: Revive 1990s smart-pixel optical interconnect. Each sense-amp group drives a micro-LED or electro-absorption modulator on the memory die's backside, and a microlens array images the whole open page onto a photodetector array on the stacked processor, moving thousands of bits in parallel with no TSVs or serializers.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and serializer periphery, targeting <0.5 pJ/bit versus 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM (fact 5).

title: Bubble swap-gate sense amps exchange two rows in one cycle
idea: Bubble memories used swap gates to trade a bit between a minor loop and the major loop in one operation. Give each sense amp a second small latch: one activation senses row A into latch 1, the next senses row B into latch 2, and each is restored into the other's row. Two rows swap in two activations without data leaving the chip.
why: Makes in-DRAM row migration cheap for row-hammer mitigation (fact 9) and hot/cold placement, replacing large TRR counter tables with swap-based remapping at ~10x lower mitigation energy.

title: Selectron binary-stripe decoders coded by one depletion implant
idea: RCA's 1946 Selectron picked one of 256 spots with crossed bars driven by binary address pairs. Build each row decoder as a pitch-matched series chain of array-style transistors under true/complement address stripes. The single added depletion-implant mask makes chosen transistors always-on, so the implant pattern alone encodes each row's address.
why: Row decoders at array pitch built from array transistors are ~3x smaller (fact 7), with one non-critical implant mask and no EUV (fact 4).

title: Core-rope weaving: per-die e-beam via layer hardwires repairs
idea: Apollo's core-rope ROM was woven by hand, each wire passing through or around each core. After wafer sort at the via-2 level, a maskless multi-beam e-beam writes one custom via layer per die that hardwires spare rows and columns into place. That layer is the one added 'mask', and no physical mask exists.
why: Deletes fuse banks, fuse latches and address-compare logic (~3-5% of die, fact 7) and power-up fuse loading, so repaired addresses take no extra latency.

title: One base-implant mask revives BiCMOS bipolar sense amps
idea: 1990s BiCMOS DRAMs used bipolar sense amps because Vbe matches to ~1 mV, against ~15 mV of MOS Vt mismatch. Add one p-base implant mask to the periphery flow to form vertical NPNs (the existing n-well as collector, existing n+ as emitter) and place a bipolar differential pre-amp in front of each latch group.
why: ~5-10x lower offset lets the amp resolve ~20 mV instead of ~100 mV, so Cs can shrink ~3x (fact 1) or bitlines can double in length, halving sense stripes (fact 7).

title: Thyristor latch wordline drivers from one implant
idea: Revive the thyratron, in its SCR form, as a wordline driver. One added implant mask forms a PNPN stack at each sub-wordline end. A tiny decoder pulse triggers it, it latches the wordline high from a pulsed 3 V rail, and it resets when the rail drops at precharge, so no level shifter or large thick-oxide PMOS is needed.
why: Sub-wordline driver stripes, a major periphery block, shrink ~2-3x (fact 7) and level shifters disappear (fact 10).

title: Stepwise wordline charging from cell-capacitor tank banks
idea: Revive 1990s adiabatic stepwise charging. Each wordline rises to 3 V in 6 steps through switches to tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages and falls back through them, recovering most of its CV² energy. The tanks are dummy DRAM cell-capacitor arrays reused in the periphery, so the only added mask is a block mask that opens the storage-node module there.
why: Wordline switching energy falls ~4-6x despite the 3 V floor (fact 10). Area cost is near zero because cell capacitors give ~100 fF/µm².

title: Marx-generator local boost replaces the central VPP pump
idea: A 1924 Marx generator charges capacitors in parallel and switches them into series for a high-voltage spike. At each sub-wordline driver, three dummy cell capacitors charge to VDD in parallel during precharge and switch into series to deliver ~3 V only to the row being opened. The one added mask is a contact mask that strings them through existing array transistors.
why: Removes most of the central VPP charge pump and its global distribution (fact 7) and halves the VPP conversion loss (fact 10).

title: One-mask NEMS relays for leakage-free row decoders
idea: Revive the relay computer (Zuse's Z3) at nanoscale. Lateral electrostatic relays are patterned in an existing upper metal layer and released by a single added air-gap etch mask, giving zero-leakage, abrupt-switching pass gates for row decoders and bank power switches.
why: Zero off-state leakage in decoders and power gates cuts standby power, and moving decoding into BEOL shrinks the silicon periphery (fact 7).

title: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto-pair latches at bitline pitch
idea: The 1959 Goto pair used two series tunnel diodes as a bistable logic element. One added pocket-implant mask forms p++/n++ Esaki junctions at each sense node, and two in series make a negative-resistance latch that resolves a bitline differential in tens of picoseconds with 2 devices instead of a 4-6 transistor cross-coupled pair.
why: The sense amp fits at 1x bitline pitch in open-bitline arrays, roughly halving the sense stripe (fact 7) and cutting latch energy.

title: Ferroelectric coercive-edge capacitor avalanches tiny bitline signals
idea: 1950s ferroelectric memories failed because switching was too easy to trigger; this turns that flaw into gain. One block mask keeps an HZO capacitor at each sense node, biased just below its coercive voltage. A 30-50 mV bitline signal tips it into switching, which dumps ~20 µC/cm² of polarization charge into the latch, and the capacitor is reset each cycle. Wear is spread across redundant capacitors.
why: ~10x charge gain at the sense node lets Cs fall toward 1-2 fF (fact 1 charge wall) with no new cell physics.

title: Widrow memistor trims sense-amp offset in one via
idea: Revive Widrow's 1960 memistor, a three-terminal electroplated resistor. One added via mask fills a Cu/GeSe electrolyte plug in each sense amp's tail leg, which is plated up or down at test (and retouched in the field) to null that amp's measured Vt offset.
why: With offset trimmed out, sense transistors can shrink to near minimum size because mismatch no longer sets W·L: ~2-3x smaller sense stripes (fact 7) and ~40% less required signal (fact 1).

title: Capacitance-collapse bitline boost from one varactor implant
idea: Echoing 1950s varactor parametric amplifiers, each bitline gets a strip of MOS varactor, formed by one added accumulation-well implant mask, held in its high-capacitance state during charge sharing. Just before latching it is switched to depletion, roughly halving total bitline capacitance, so with charge conserved the differential voltage about doubles with no transistor noise.
why: Doubles sense signal (facts 1, 8), allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines with half the sense stripes (fact 7).

title: Charge-transfer preamplifier revived with one low-Vt implant
idea: The charge-transfer sense schemes of 1970s DRAMs moved bitline charge through a near-threshold transistor onto a tiny node. One added low-Vt implant mask makes pitch-matched transfer gates that, biased at threshold, pass the cell's signal charge from a ~60 fF bitline onto a ~4 fF node, multiplying voltage swing ~5-10x before the latch.
why: Large signal gain (fact 1) permits 3D DRAM tiers with ~1-2 fF capacitors (fact 2) or 2-4x longer bitlines with fewer sense amps (fact 7).

title: Delay-line wave-pipelined data bus on one thick RDL layer
idea: Mercury delay lines stored bits as pulses in flight. One added thick-copper redistribution layer, which reuses existing pad openings as vias, carries low-loss global data lines with 3-4 bits in flight at once (wave pipelining, used in 1960s IBM machines) and no intermediate pipeline latches or repeaters.
why: Triples global-bus throughput per wire, removes repeater and latch stripes (fact 7) and cuts global-data energy ~30% (fact 5).

title: Tape-style run-length coding lets bitlines pack tighter
idea: Magnetic tape used run-length-limited codes to avoid worst-case flux patterns. Add a 64b/68b write encoder that forbids the worst bitline coupling patterns, such as a lone 1 between 0s on adjacent bitlines of one row, so sense amps never see the worst aggressor sums. No mask is added at all.
why: Worst-case coupling noise drops ~40%, allowing ~20-25% tighter bitline pitch or less margin (facts 1, 4) for 6% capacity overhead.

title: Chopper-measured sense offsets stored in a per-stripe trim row
idea: 1940s chopper-stabilized amplifiers swapped their inputs to cancel drift. During refresh slots each sense amp's inputs are shorted and swapped and its decisions counted, giving a 2-bit offset estimate per amp. The estimates are kept in a dedicated trim row and loaded into per-amp dynamic trim capacitors, which are rewritten with each refresh. Zero added masks.
why: Mismatch-driven sense-amp area halves (fact 7) and margin improves ~30 mV, extending bitlines or shrinking Cs (fact 1).

title: Bubble-memory boot loop replaces the fuse module entirely
idea: Bubble chips kept their own bad-loop map in an on-chip boot loop read at power-up. Store the redundancy map in the module's existing SPD EEPROM or the controller's NVM, and stream it into the die's repair latches during initialization over the mode-register interface. Laser and e-fuse blocks and their process steps go away, a net reduction in masks.
why: Removes fuse arrays and programming circuits (~2-4% of die, fact 7) and lets repairs be updated in the field.

title: Dekatron token ring scans refresh with no counter or decoder
idea: Dekatron counting tubes moved a glow one cathode per pulse. Thread a one-hot token through a 2-transistor dynamic shift chain built into the sub-wordline driver stripe, like an LCD gate driver. Each refresh pulse fires the token's row and passes the token on, so refresh needs no address counter, no internal address mux and no decoder toggling. Zero masks added.
why: Cuts refresh energy ~20-30% by not toggling decoder trees (fact 3) and removes refresh-address logic (fact 7).

title: Core-memory coincident selection from one shield-strip cut mask
idea: Core memory switched only the bit where X and Y half-currents coincided. One added cut mask splits the inter-channel shield (back-gate) plate of a vertical-channel array into strips that run along the bitline direction, one strip per 1/16 of a row. A cell turns on only when its row wordline and its segment strip are both raised, and each alone is subthreshold.
why: Only the addressed 1/16 of a row dumps charge and is sensed, cutting the 128x overfetch to ~8x (fact 8) and activation energy ~10x, and it shrinks the row-hammer blast radius (fact 9).

title: Williams-tube pickup plate: segmented cell plate becomes the sensor
idea: The Williams tube read every spot through one pickup plate over the tube face. One added plate-cut mask divides the common cell plate into tiles, each wired to a charge amplifier in the CMOS under the array. When a cell is accessed, its charge redistribution appears on its tile, so one amplifier per tile can read any cell for scrubbing, retention profiling and low-bandwidth reads without firing the bitline sense-amp row.
why: Background operations skip the 8 kb page activation, ~100x less energy per scrubbed bit (fact 8), and enable per-row adaptive refresh (fact 3).

title: Vacuum nanogap transistors as oxide-free high-voltage drivers
idea: Revive the vacuum tube at 50 nm. One added cavity mask etches a nanogap between a sharp source tip and the drain under an existing gate, and a non-conformal oxide deposition pinches it shut under vacuum. Field emission across a gap shorter than the electron mean free path switches with no gate-oxide stress and tolerates 3-5 V at minimum size.
why: Wordline and pump switches no longer need large thick-oxide HV transistors (facts 7, 10), so driver area could shrink ~3x; a radiation-hard bonus for space.

title: Geiger-tube avalanche junction amplifies bitline charge
idea: Like a Geiger-Müller tube or a modern SPAD: one added implant mask forms a high-field p+/n junction at each sense node, biased just below breakdown, with the bitline voltage setting its reverse bias. The signal's sign decides whether impact-ionization multiplication (~10-50x) happens before the latch fires, and the junction is then quenched.
why: Charge gain at the sense node (fact 1) supports smaller cells or longer bitlines with ~2 extra devices per sense amp (fact 7).

title: Core-plane diagonal sense wire becomes a noise-reference bitline
idea: Core-memory sense wires ran diagonally so half-select noise from every drive line canceled. Route one dummy bitline per mat diagonally across all bitlines in existing metal, with at most one via-mask change. It picks up the same wordline kick and coupling noise as the real bitlines and serves as a live reference subtracted at each sense-amp group.
why: Removes common-mode wordline-coupling noise ~3x for ~20-30 mV more margin (fact 1), which also allows a lower VARY (fact 10).

title: Core inhibit-wire counter-pulse cancels row-hammer disturbance
idea: Core memory's inhibit winding sent an opposing current to cancel unwanted switching. When a row activates, its two neighbor wordlines get a synchronized, shaped negative counter-pulse from the same sub-wordline driver, cross-wired in existing metal with no added mask. The pulse cancels the capacitive kick and electron-injection field that cause hammer flips.
why: Raises the row-hammer threshold from ~1k toward 10k+ activations (fact 9), shrinking or eliminating on-die TRR counter tables (fact 7).
